# Preface {.unnumbered}

When we look across science and engineering, artificial intelligence has begun to do real work. It searches design spaces too vast to enumerate by hand, learns predictive models where first principles cannot easily reach, proposes candidate solutions, and verifies complex results. But can AI also transform how we design computing systems and silicon chips?

Computer architecture is an unusually demanding domain to test that question. An architectural decision begins with high-level workload intent and propagates through software runtimes, ISAs, microarchitectures, RTL, and physical silicon signoff. Our measurements are expensive and inherently partial. A simulator, compiler, formal model, synthesis report, and post-layout analysis each reveal a different slice of the system under different operating assumptions. Verification must prove far more than whether a candidate design looks plausible, and a logic bug discovered after tapeout carries catastrophic financial and schedule costs compared to a software patch.

Yet that very difficulty is why our opportunity as architects is so compelling. Rather than relying on isolated CAD automation scripts or prompt-based code generation, an *AI-native system and chip design methodology* unifies the target substrate and the engineering life cycle. It connects machine-inspectable state representations, closed-loop neural surrogates, and evaluator-owned signoff anchors so that autonomous agent loops co-design hardware and software together. However, automated generators can also produce candidate designs far faster than our teams can responsibly evaluate. Generating options faster helps only when our engineering process can determine what those options mean.

This book makes that capability concrete without assuming its automated success. The ambition is deliberately larger than generating RTL from a prompt or training a standalone performance predictor. It asks whether a complete, closed-loop approach can produce superior architectures, reduce the total cost of reaching a comparable result, or achieve both. It does not assume that this moonshot is solved; it establishes the foundational principles and tool harnesses required to pursue it rigorously without confusing local progress with full-system success.

The architecture problem always comes first. Depending on the design problem, the right approach may combine generation, prediction, optimization, conventional analysis, or no AI at all. Architecture 2.0 is not a claim that every design task requires machine learning; it is a framework to determine where AI earns its place and what evidence its use must produce.

## On the Title of This Book {.unnumbered}

The title of this book, *Architecture 2.0: Principles of AI-Native System and Chip Design*, reflects the exact scope and philosophy of this work. None of its terms are arbitrary.

Architecture 2.0 marks a paradigm shift[^fn-paradigm-shift-c00] away from manual point-design sweeps toward autonomous, closed-loop exploration across the hardware-software stack. The book focuses on *Principles* rather than *Foundations* because it is not a passive theoretical treatise; it is a practical guide to the decision-making rules, evidence standards, and design trade-offs that architects face every day.

[^fn-paradigm-shift-c00]: **Author's note**: I do not use the term *paradigm shift* lightly. In Thomas Kuhn's classic formulation (*The Structure of Scientific Revolutions*, 1962), a paradigm shift occurs when a discipline's established methods encounter physical and operational limits that incremental improvements can no longer resolve [@Kuhn1962ScientificRevolutions]. Architecture 2.0 represents precisely such a shift for computer architecture.

In this book, *AI-Native* has a precise engineering definition (building the entire exploration workflow, data representation contracts, and verification harnesses natively around closed-loop AI search, rather than treating AI as an isolated copilot retrofitted onto individual design tasks). Finally, *System and Chip Design* reflects the physical reality of modern architecture: a silicon chip cannot be designed in isolation from the software compilers, memory hierarchies, interconnects, and physical signoff engines that surround it.

## What This Book Teaches {.unnumbered}

This book follows an architecture question through the engineering work required to answer it. As architects, we formulate the question and represent the design state, then select the methods and run the tools required to evaluate candidate solutions. What the tools return must be interpreted, compared against credible baselines, and turned into a technical recommendation that a human authority will own. This sequence keeps the focus on what architects must judge and execute rather than on any ephemeral model or tool.

When we evaluate whether adopting an automated workflow improves a design program, the object of study is the complete human-and-tool workflow. Candidate quality, final architecture performance, and the specific contribution of an AI model require separate, rigorous tests. A powerful model can sit inside a broken design loop, whereas a modest learned method can yield immense value if it eliminates the exact bottleneck constraining our decisions. As you complete this book, you will be prepared to execute the following core architectural duties:

- **Formulate architecture questions** and clarify the specific decisions they support.
- **Diagnose limiting bottlenecks** in a workflow before selecting an AI or conventional method.
- **Represent design state**, cross-layer dependencies, permitted modification spaces, and unrepresented unknowns.
- **Select appropriate methods** among conventional analysis, unassisted design, candidate generation, performance prediction, design space optimization, or targeted hybrids.
- **Interface methods to executable tools**, reconstruct execution trajectories, and qualify which tool outputs constitute valid physical measurements.
- **Evaluate outcomes fairly**, isolating the architecture result and the contribution of AI against matched baselines at equal evaluation budgets.
- **Defend technical recommendations**, explicitly stating evidence limits while identifying who holds commitment authority and who retains ultimate technical responsibility.

To keep these principles concrete, this book uses a recurring Lighthouse case study featuring a real-time mobile extended reality compute subsystem under strict power and physical constraints. Nothing in that subsystem can be solved in isolation. The power envelope limits the accelerator, the accelerator reshapes memory traffic, and the memory hierarchy shifts thermal density across the die. The book returns to this Lighthouse case whenever the case exposes a fundamental principle, grounding the methods in executable reality rather than abstract claims.

This book sits at the convergence of three established technical disciplines, as shown in @fig-book-composition.

![**Architecture 2.0 unifies computer architecture, machine learning, and EDA.** Computer architecture supplies the questions and design tradeoffs, machine learning supplies methods for learning and search, and EDA supplies executable implementation and analysis tools together with tool-derived evidence or estimates about physical constraints. Work at their intersection must satisfy the relevant standards of all three.](../../images/fig-book-composition){#fig-book-composition width="88%" fig-alt="Three-circle Venn diagram of computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation, with Architecture 2.0 at their intersection"}

Computer architecture and machine learning intersect in ML for systems, where learned models predict performance and explore design spaces. Computer architecture and EDA intersect in chip design, where microarchitectural choices become RTL and physical floorplans. Machine learning and EDA intersect in ML for CAD, which accelerates placement, routing, and logic verification. Architecture 2.0 operates where all three meet.

This intersection matters because each discipline enforces distinct evidence standards. Simulation benchmarks validate work between architecture and machine learning; physical signoff and silicon validate work between architecture and EDA; post-route metrics validate work between machine learning and EDA. Architecture 2.0 demands that we satisfy all three standards simultaneously. A generated hardware block that ignores workload characteristics is not an architecture result; a learned estimate that fails physical signoff is not a physical result; and a successful tool run without a matched baseline comparison does not prove that AI improved the design.

This book is not a catalog of current neural networks, a prompt-to-chip automation script, or a defense of using AI indiscriminately. It does not replace architectural judgment, compiler engineering, or formal verification with black-box models. Physical checks remain paramount, and named human architects remain answerable for the choices made and the silicon committed.

## Who This Book Is For {.unnumbered}

The primary audience is the practicing computer architect and systems researcher. This book assumes familiarity with performance, power, energy, area, and hardware-software interfaces, as well as the ability to evaluate architecture papers, simulator logs, and synthesis reports. It does not assume prior background in machine learning; it introduces all necessary ML concepts through concrete architecture problems and physical constraints.

Four technical communities meet at this intersection, and this book is structured to serve each of them:

- **Computer architects** seeking to integrate AI generation and search into rigorous design space exploration without losing control of physical constraints.
- **EDA and CAD engineers** looking to connect synthesis, placement, and verification tools to high-level architectural decision loops.
- **Machine learning and ML-systems researchers** entering hardware design who need to understand how physical signoff, evaluation costs, and formal verification redefine the criteria for a valid result.
- **Graduate students and systems engineers** spanning hardware and software who want a shared vocabulary and rigorous framework for AI-assisted systems engineering.

The common test across all four communities is whether we can apply this reasoning to new architecture problems beyond the Lighthouse case, recognizing when an AI-assisted loop excels and when conventional engineering remains superior.

## Book Structure {.unnumbered}

This book develops its engineering argument across four sequential movements:

- **Part I: System Intent and Design Lifecycles** defines what a complete Architecture 2.0 capability must achieve, exposing why candidate generation velocity must be paired with explicit evaluation capacity. It establishes the 8-layer prompt stack and 6-stage lifecycle required to translate compact intent into verifiable hardware specifications.
- **Part II: Technical Building Blocks** details the four sub-assemblies of our technical substrate. It traces an architecture question through state representations, learned search methods, containerized tool environments, and verification feedback, establishing how these modular building blocks preserve physical meaning during automated search.
- **Part III: Closed-Loop Execution and Ownership** demonstrates how end-to-end design workflows run across spatial accelerators and memory subsystems. It evaluates workflow efficiency without bias, addresses selective requalification across target shifts, and establishes that 100 percent In-Order Commit Authority remains strictly with human architects.
- **Part IV: Open Infrastructure and Ecosystems** changes altitude to address discipline-wide scaling. It details the open data schemas, OpenROAD signoff telemetry, cloud silicon shuttles, and consortium benchmarks required to make AI-assisted architecture claims open and reproducible.

Together, these four movements carry the argument from high-level vision to executable methods that you can evaluate, apply, and transfer across diverse system design challenges, and then to the shared foundations the discipline still needs.

## How to Read This Book {.unnumbered}

Read this book sequentially on your first pass. The engineering argument is cumulative. Method selection depends on state representation, measurement validity depends on tool execution discipline, and technical recommendations depend on evidence limits. The Lighthouse mobile XR case study provides narrative continuity throughout, serving as a concrete reference rather than a rigid design template.

As you read, test these principles against your own design problems. Ask what decision truly matters, what hidden constraints must be exposed, which baseline comparison is fair, what your tools actually measured, and what risks remain unverified. Abstracting these principles beyond specific examples is the true test of architectural mastery.

Specific AI models, benchmark scores, and CAD tool interfaces will evolve rapidly over time. The core reasoning in this book is built to outlast them. When we ground the work in problem formulation, state representation, tool discipline, rigorous evaluation, and human commitment authority, we can swap out every model and tool named here without losing the underlying architectural framework.

AI will fundamentally reshape system and chip design, but candidate generation alone will not drive that revolution. The future of our discipline belongs to design systems that connect high-level intent to verifiable physical evidence, and to architects who possess the judgment to govern them. Architecture 2.0 provides the disciplined foundation to decide where AI belongs, where it does not, what the evidence proves, and how we build next-generation computing systems.
